prompt: According to the rules for resonance forms, which statement about individual resonance forms is true?

choices.text: They are imaginary; the real structure is a composite, or resonance hybrid, of the forms
Each is a real structure that exists for part of the time
choices.why: Species such as acetate don't switch back and forth between forms; they have single, unchanging structures.

choices.text: Only the most stable one is real
choices.why: No single form is real. Even nonequivalent forms all contribute to the hybrid.

choices.text: They are different compounds that can be separated
choices.why: They are different drawings of one substance, not different substances.

explanation: Rule 1: individual resonance forms are imaginary, not real. The real structure is a composite, or resonance hybrid, of the different forms. Species such as acetate and benzene differ from other substances only in the way they are represented in drawings.

prompt: Which change is allowed when going from one resonance form to another?

choices.text: Moving a lone pair or π electrons to a new position
Moving a hydrogen atom to a different atom
choices.why: The position of every atom stays the same; only π or nonbonding electrons move.

choices.text: Changing a carbon from sp^2 to sp^3
choices.why: Neither the position nor the hybridization of any atom changes between resonance forms.

choices.text: Breaking a σ bond so that two atoms are no longer connected
choices.why: Resonance forms differ only in π or nonbonding electrons; the σ framework and connections are unchanged.

explanation: Rule 2: resonance forms differ only in the placement of their π or nonbonding electrons. Neither the position nor the hybridization of any atom changes from one resonance form to another.

prompt: How is the carbon atom bonded to the two oxygens in the acetate ion hybridized in its two resonance forms?

choices.text: sp^2 in both forms
sp^2 in one form and sp^3 in the other
choices.why: Hybridization never changes between resonance forms; the carbon is sp^2 in both.

choices.text: sp^3 in both forms
choices.why: This carbon has a C=O double bond in each form, and the book states it is sp^2-hybridized.

choices.text: sp in both forms
choices.why: sp goes with triple bonds, as in acetylene; this carbon is sp^2.

explanation: In the acetate ion, the carbon atom is sp^2-hybridized and the oxygen atoms remain in exactly the same place in both resonance forms. Only the π electrons of the C=O bond and the lone-pair electrons on oxygen are placed differently.

prompt: Which electrons are placed differently in the two resonance forms of the acetate ion?

choices.text: The π electrons of the C=O bond and the lone-pair electrons on oxygen
The σ electrons of the C–O bonds
choices.why: The σ bonds are the same in both forms; only π and nonbonding electrons move.

choices.text: The electrons of the C–H bonds
choices.why: The CH3 group is unchanged; the electrons that move are on the CO2 part.

choices.text: The electrons of the C–C bond
choices.why: That σ bond is identical in both forms.

explanation: In acetate, only the positions of the π electrons in the C=O bond and the lone-pair electrons on oxygen differ from one resonance form to another. The movement can be shown with curved arrows.

prompt: What does a curved arrow between resonance forms always indicate?

choices.text: The movement of electrons
The movement of atoms
choices.why: A curved arrow never shows atoms moving; atoms stay in place between resonance forms.

choices.text: The movement of a proton
choices.why: A proton is an atom's nucleus; curved arrows here show electrons only.

choices.text: A change in hybridization
choices.why: Hybridization doesn't change between resonance forms. The arrow shows where electrons go.

explanation: The movement of electrons from one resonance structure to another can be indicated with curved arrows. A curved arrow always indicates the movement of electrons, not the movement of atoms.

prompt: In a curved arrow, which way do the electrons move?

choices.text: From the atom or bond at the tail to the atom or bond at the head
From the head of the arrow to the tail
choices.why: It's the reverse: electrons start at the tail and end at the arrowhead.

choices.text: In both directions at once
choices.why: A curved arrow has one head and shows one direction of electron movement.

choices.text: Toward the atom with the positive charge only
choices.why: The arrow can point to any atom or bond; electrons go from tail to head.

explanation: A curved arrow shows that a pair of electrons moves from the atom or bond at the tail of the arrow to the atom or bond at the head of the arrow.

prompt: How many electrons does one curved arrow, as used for resonance forms, show moving?
explanation: A curved arrow shows that a pair of electrons, two electrons, moves from the atom or bond at its tail to the atom or bond at its head.

prompt: What moves when curved arrows are drawn between the two resonance forms of benzene?

choices.text: Only the π electrons of the double bonds
The carbon atoms, which shift to new positions
choices.why: The carbon and hydrogen atoms remain in place; only electrons move.

choices.text: The hydrogen atoms, which move around the ring
choices.why: Atoms never move between resonance forms.

choices.text: The σ electrons of the C–H bonds
choices.why: Only π or nonbonding electrons change position between resonance forms.

explanation: The situation with benzene is similar to that with acetate: the π electrons in the double bonds move, as shown with curved arrows, but the carbon and hydrogen atoms remain in place.

prompt: Must all resonance forms of a substance be equivalent?

choices.text: No; nonequivalent forms can exist, and all of them contribute to the resonance hybrid
Yes; if two structures aren't equivalent, they aren't resonance forms
choices.why: Rule 3 says resonance forms don't have to be equivalent; the acetone anion has two nonequivalent forms.

choices.text: No, but only the most stable form contributes to the hybrid
choices.why: Even nonequivalent forms both contribute; the hybrid just resembles the more stable one more.

choices.text: Yes, because resonance forms must have the charge on the same atom
choices.why: In the acetone anion, one form has the negative charge on carbon and the other on oxygen.

explanation: Rule 3: different resonance forms of a substance don't have to be equivalent. The anion of acetone has two nonequivalent resonance forms, and both contribute to the overall resonance hybrid.

prompt: Acetone reacts with a strong base to form an anion with two resonance forms. Which describes them?

choices.text: One has a C=O bond and the negative charge on carbon; the other has a C=C bond and the negative charge on oxygen
Both have a C=O bond, with the negative charge on a different carbon in each
choices.why: In one form the electrons move to make a carbon–carbon double bond and put the charge on oxygen.

choices.text: Both have the negative charge on oxygen, with the C=O bond on different sides
choices.why: That pattern fits acetate. The acetone anion's forms put the charge on carbon in one and on oxygen in the other.

choices.text: One has a C=O bond and the other has a hydrogen moved to oxygen
choices.why: Moving a hydrogen changes an atom's position, which never happens between resonance forms.

explanation: The acetone anion has two resonance forms: one contains a carbon–oxygen double bond and has a negative charge on carbon; the other contains a carbon–carbon double bond and has a negative charge on oxygen. They aren't equivalent, but both contribute to the hybrid.

prompt: Which resonance form should the true structure of the acetone anion resemble more?

choices.text: The form with the negative charge on oxygen, because oxygen is electronegative
The form with the negative charge on carbon, because carbon is the less electronegative atom
choices.why: A negative charge is more stable on the more electronegative atom, oxygen, so that form is more stable.

choices.text: Both equally, because all resonance forms contribute equally
choices.why: When forms are nonequivalent, the hybrid resembles the more stable form.

choices.text: The form with the C=O bond, because acetone itself has a C=O bond
choices.why: The form with the C=O bond puts the charge on carbon, the less stable arrangement.

explanation: When two resonance forms are nonequivalent, the actual hybrid resembles the more stable form. So the acetone anion should be more like the form that places the negative charge on the electronegative oxygen atom rather than on carbon.

prompt: A proposed structure for the acetate ion shows the central carbon with five bonds. Why is it not a valid resonance form?

choices.text: The carbon would have ten valence electrons, breaking the octet rule
It places the negative charge on carbon
choices.why: A charge on carbon is allowed, as in the acetone anion. The problem is the five bonds.

choices.text: The two oxygens are now equivalent
choices.why: Equivalence isn't what makes it invalid; resonance forms must obey normal valence rules.

choices.text: Resonance forms may not contain two double bonds
choices.why: Benzene's resonance forms each have three double bonds. The issue is carbon's ten electrons.

explanation: Rule 4: resonance forms obey normal rules of valency, and the octet rule still applies to second-row, main-group atoms. The structure is invalid because its carbon atom has five bonds and ten valence electrons.

prompt: In a valid resonance form, what is the most valence electrons a second-row, main-group atom such as carbon can have?
explanation: Resonance forms obey normal rules of valency: the octet rule still applies to second-row, main-group atoms. A carbon with five bonds would have ten valence electrons, so such a structure is not a valid resonance form.

prompt: How does the stability of a resonance hybrid compare with that of its individual resonance forms?

choices.text: The hybrid is more stable than any individual form
The hybrid is as stable as its most stable form
choices.why: Resonance itself adds stability, so the hybrid is more stable than even the best single form.

choices.text: The hybrid is less stable, because its electrons are spread out
choices.why: Spreading electrons out over more of the molecule is what makes it more stable.

choices.text: The hybrid's stability is the average of its forms
choices.why: Resonance leads to stability: the hybrid is more stable than any individual form.

explanation: Rule 5: the resonance hybrid is more stable than any individual resonance form. In other words, resonance leads to stability.

prompt: Why is a substance with more resonance forms generally more stable?

choices.text: Its electrons are spread over a larger part of the molecule and are closer to more nuclei
It switches between more structures, so it spends less time in any unstable one
choices.why: Resonance forms are imaginary; the substance has one unchanging structure and doesn't switch.

choices.text: Its atoms can move into more favorable positions
choices.why: Atoms don't move between resonance forms; only π and nonbonding electrons are placed differently.

choices.text: It has more electrons in total
choices.why: Every resonance form has the same electrons; they are just spread out more in the hybrid.

explanation: Generally speaking, the larger the number of resonance forms a substance has, the more stable it is, because its electrons are spread out over a larger part of the molecule and are closer to more nuclei. A benzene ring, for instance, is more stable because of resonance than might otherwise be expected.
